chapters.title: הַחִפּוּשׂ אַחַר הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה
chapters.orig_title: The Search for the Wicked Witch

w: שׁוֹמֵר הַשְּׁעָרִים|the Guardian of the Gates
s.line: The soldier with the green whiskers led them through the streets of the Emerald City until they reached the room where the Guardian of the Gates lived.
s.note: זָקָן (zakan) = a beard; זָקֵן (zaken) = an old man. Without niqqud both are written זקן, and only context tells you which one is meant. שֶׁבּוֹ = "in which": שֶׁ + בּוֹ (in it), the normal way to say "where" after a place noun.

s.line: This officer unlocked their spectacles to put them back in his great box,
s.note: לְהַחְזִיר (hif'il) = to put back, to return something; לַחְזֹר (pa'al) = to come back yourself. You will hear תַּחְזִיר לִי אֶת זֶה (give that back to me) all the time.

s.line: and then he politely opened the gate for our friends.
s.note: Hebrew makes many adverbs from בְּ + an abstract noun: בַּאֲדִיבוּת (politely), בְּשִׂמְחָה (gladly), בִּזְהִירוּת (carefully).

w: הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמַּעֲרָב|the Wicked Witch of the West
s.line: “Which road leads to the Wicked Witch of the West?” asked Dorothy.
s.note: דֶּרֶךְ is usually feminine, so it is אֵיזוֹ and מוֹבִילָה, not אֵיזֶה / מוֹבִיל.

w: שׁוֹמֵר הַשְּׁעָרִים|the Guardian of the Gates
s.line: “There is no road,” answered the Guardian of the Gates.
“No one ever wishes to go that way.”
s.note: לְשָׁם = "to there", for movement toward a place; שָׁם = there (location). Hebrew keeps the two apart, like לְאָן (where to?) and אֵיפֹה (where?).

s.line: “How, then, are we to find her?” inquired the girl.
s.note: נִמְצָא here is the future of pa'al: "we will find". The same letters also spell the nif'al נִמְצָא, "is found / is located", which comes up later in this chapter.

s.line: “That will be easy,” replied the man, “for when she knows you are in the country of the Winkies she will find you, and make you all her slaves.”
s.note: הָפַךְ אֶת X לְ־Y = to turn X into Y: הוּא הָפַךְ אֶת הַחֶדֶר לְמִשְׂרָד (he turned the room into an office). Note כְּשֶׁהִיא תֵּדַע: after כְּשֶׁ Hebrew uses the future when the time is future, where English uses the present ("when she knows").

s.line: “Perhaps not,” said the Scarecrow, “for we mean to destroy her.”
s.note: מִתְכַּוֵּן לְ־ = to intend to, and also "to mean": לְמָה אַתָּה מִתְכַּוֵּן? (what do you mean?). לְהַשְׁמִיד = to destroy, wipe out; a strong word, common in the news.

w: זֶה כְּבָר סִפּוּר אַחֵר|that's a different story|~idiom
שׁוֹמֵר הַשְּׁעָרִים|the Guardian of the Gates
s.line: “Oh, that is different,” said the Guardian of the Gates.
s.note: זֶה כְּבָר סִפּוּר אַחֵר = "that's another story", the everyday way to say that something changes the picture.

s.line: “No one has ever destroyed her before, so I naturally thought she would make slaves of you, as she has of the rest.
s.note: עוֹד לֹא = not yet. כַּמּוּבָן = of course, from מוּבָן (understood). הַשְּׁאָר = the rest, the others; וְכָל הַשְּׁאָר = "and all the rest".

s.line: But take care; for she is wicked and fierce, and may not allow you to destroy her.
s.note: נִזְהַר (nif'al, active meaning) = to be careful; תִּזָּהֵר! = watch out! יִתָּכֵן שֶׁ = "it may be that", a slightly formal alternative to אוּלַי. הִרְשָׁה לְ־ = to allow someone; רִשְׁיוֹן (licence) is from the same root.

s.line: Keep to the West, where the sun sets, and you cannot fail to find her.”
s.note: מַעֲרָבָה = westward: the ending ָה marks direction, as in הַבַּיְתָה (homeward) and צָפוֹנָה (northward). In speech the future תַּמְשִׁיכוּ often serves as a polite imperative.

s.line: They thanked him and bade him good-bye, and turned toward the West,
s.note: נִפְרַד מִ־ = to say goodbye to, to part from (nif'al, active meaning). הוֹדָה לְ־ = to thank someone; the everyday תּוֹדָה comes from the same root.

s.line: walking over fields of soft grass dotted here and there with daisies and buttercups.
s.note: מְנֻקָּד (pu'al) = dotted, and also "pointed" with niqqud: a טֶקְסְט מְנֻקָּד is a text like this one. פֹּה וָשָׁם = here and there; note the old form וָ for "and" in this fixed phrase.

w: שֶׁלָּבְשָׁה|that she had put on|pa'al · ל־ב־שׁ
s.line: Dorothy still wore the pretty silk dress she had put on in the palace,
but now, to her surprise, she found it was no longer green, but pure white.
s.note: Reported speech keeps the original tense: "she found that the dress is no longer green" (כְּבָר לֹא יְרֻקָּה). כְּבָר לֹא = no longer. אֶלָּא = "but rather", used after a negative: לֹא X אֶלָּא Y.

s.line: The ribbon around Toto’s neck had also lost its green color and was as white as Dorothy’s dress.
s.note: סֶרֶט = a ribbon, but today mostly a film: הָלַכְנוּ לַסֶּרֶט (we went to the movie). אִבֵּד (pi'el) = to lose; הָלַךְ לְאִבּוּד = got lost.

s.line: The Emerald City was soon left far behind.
s.note: עִיר is feminine, so the verb is נִשְׁאֲרָה. English "was left behind" becomes the active nif'al נִשְׁאַר (remained).

w: כְּכָל שֶׁהִתְקַדְּמוּ|the further they went|~כְּכָל שֶׁ־ = the more …
s.line: As they advanced the ground became rougher and hillier,
s.note: כְּכָל שֶׁ = "the more / the further …": כְּכָל שֶׁהִתְקַדְּמוּ = the further they went. הִתְקַדֵּם (hitpa'el) = to advance, make progress. נַעֲשָׂה = became, the nif'al of עָשָׂה.

s.line: for there were no farms nor houses in this country of the West, and the ground was untilled.
s.note: עִבֵּד (pi'el) = to till the soil, and in modern use "to process": עִבּוּד נְתוּנִים (data processing), מָזוֹן מְעֻבָּד (processed food).

s.line: In the afternoon the sun shone hot in their faces, for there were no trees to offer them shade;
s.note: הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ קוֹפַחַת is the stock phrase for a blazing sun, heard every summer in Israel. אַחַר הַצָּהֳרַיִם = afternoon, often shortened in writing to אחה״צ.

s.line: so that before night Dorothy and Toto and the Lion were tired, and lay down upon the grass and fell asleep, with the Woodman and the Scarecrow keeping watch.
s.note: שָׁמַר עַל = to guard, look after: תִּשְׁמֹר עַל עַצְמְךָ (take care of yourself). Without עַל, שָׁמַר + object means "to keep, save": שָׁמַרְתִּי אֶת הַקַּבָּלָה (I kept the receipt).

w: לַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמַּעֲרָב|the Wicked Witch of the West (had)
s.line: Now the Wicked Witch of the West had but one eye, yet that was as powerful as a telescope, and could see everywhere.
s.note: עַיִן is feminine, so it is אַחַת, הִיא, חֲזָקָה and יָכְלָה. Most paired body parts are feminine: יָד, רֶגֶל, אֹזֶן. Binoculars are מִשְׁקֶפֶת, from the same root as מִשְׁקָפַיִם.

s.line: So, as she sat in the door of her castle, she happened to look around and saw Dorothy lying asleep, with her friends all about her.
s.note: הִסְתַּכֵּל is hitpa'el of ס־כ־ל. When a root begins with ס, שׁ or צ, the ת of hitpa'el swaps places with it: not *הִתְסַכֵּל but הִסְתַּכֵּל. בְּמִקְרֶה = by chance; לֹא בְּמִקְרֶה = not by accident.

s.line: They were a long distance off, but the Wicked Witch was angry to find them in her country;
so she blew upon a silver whistle that hung around her neck.
s.note: שָׁרַק = to whistle, and מַשְׁרוֹקִית = a whistle, from the same root; the referee שׁוֹרֵק at a football match. תָּלוּי = hanging, and also "it depends": זֶה תָּלוּי בְּךָ (it's up to you).

s.line: At once there came running to her from all directions a pack of great wolves.
s.note: The verb comes first and agrees with the subject that follows: הִגִּיעָה is feminine because of לַהֲקָה. לַהֲקָה is a pack of wolves or a flock of birds, but also a band or troupe: לַהֲקַת רוֹק (a rock band).

w: הָיוּ לָהֶם|they had|~lit. there were to them
s.line: They had long legs and fierce eyes and sharp teeth.
s.note: רַגְלַיִם, עֵינַיִם, שִׁנַּיִם: the dual ending ַיִם is used for things that come in pairs, and these nouns are feminine, so their adjectives end in וֹת. מְאַיֵּם = threatening; אִיּוּם = a threat, a news word.

s.line: “Go to those people,” said the Witch, “and tear them to pieces.”
s.note: קָרַע לִגְזָרִים = to tear to shreds, also used of harsh criticism: הַמְּבַקֵּר קָרַע אֶת הַסֶּרֶט לִגְזָרִים. The future תִּקְרְעוּ works here as an imperative, as it often does in speech.

s.line: “Are you not going to make them your slaves?” asked the leader of the wolves.
s.note: מַנְהִיג = a leader, from הִנְהִיג (to lead); מַנְהִיגוּת = leadership.

s.line: “No,” she answered, “one is of tin, and one of straw; one is a girl and another a Lion.
s.note: עָשׂוּי מִ־ = made of: עָשׂוּי מֵעֵץ (made of wood). Notice אַחַת for the girl and אֶחָד for the others: "one" agrees in gender with whoever it stands for.

s.line: None of them is fit to work, so you may tear them into small pieces.”
s.note: מַתְאִים = suitable, fits: זֶה לֹא מַתְאִים לִי (that doesn't suit me / doesn't work for me). חֲתִיכָה = a piece; in slang it also means a good-looking person.

s.line: “Very well,” said the wolf, and he dashed away at full speed, followed by the others.
s.note: בִּמְלוֹא = "in the fullness of", "with full …": בִּמְלוֹא הַמְּהִירוּת (at full speed), בִּמְלוֹא הַכֹּחַ (with all one's strength). זִנֵּק = to leap, dash; prices and numbers מְזַנְּקִים in the news.

s.line: It was lucky the Scarecrow and the Woodman were wide awake and heard the wolves coming.
s.note: לְמַזָּלָם = luckily for them, from מַזָּל (luck): לְמַזָּלִי (luckily for me), לְמַרְבֵּה הַמַּזָּל (fortunately). עֵר = awake; הִתְעוֹרֵר = to wake up.

s.line: “This is my fight,” said the Woodman, “so get behind me and I will meet them as they come.”
He seized his axe, which he had made very sharp,
s.note: הִשְׁחִיז (hif'il) = to sharpen a blade; a pencil sharpener is מְחַדֵּד. תָּפַס = to grab, catch, and in speech "to get it": לֹא תָּפַסְתִּי (I didn't catch that).

s.line: and as the leader of the wolves came on the Tin Woodman swung his arm and chopped the wolf’s head from its body, so that it immediately died.
s.note: הִסְתָּעֵר עַל = to charge at, storm; another hitpa'el where ס and ת swap. הֵנִיף = to swing or raise high; הֵנִיף דֶּגֶל = to raise a flag.

s.line: As soon as he could raise his axe another wolf came up, and he also fell under the sharp edge of the Tin Woodman’s weapon.
s.note: הִסְפִּיק = to manage (in time), one of the most useful verbs in daily speech: לֹא הִסְפַּקְתִּי לֶאֱכֹל (I didn't get a chance to eat). בְּרֶגַע שֶׁ = the moment that, as soon as.

s.line: There were forty wolves, and forty times a wolf was killed, so that at last they all lay dead in a heap before the Woodman.
s.note: נֶהֱרַג (nif'al) = was killed, the passive of הָרַג (killed). It is the standard news verb for deaths in accidents and attacks: שְׁנֵי אֲנָשִׁים נֶהֶרְגוּ בִּתְאוּנָה.

s.line: Then he put down his axe and sat beside the Scarecrow, who said, “It was a good fight, friend.”
s.note: הִנִּיחַ = to put down, set down, and also "to assume": אֲנִי מַנִּיחַ שֶׁ… (I assume that …). הִתְיַשֵּׁב = to sit down (the action), as against יָשַׁב (to be sitting).

s.line: They waited until Dorothy awoke the next morning.
s.note: לְמָחֳרָת = the next day, looking back from a past day, as in a story. Looking ahead from today, "tomorrow" is מָחָר. בַּבֹּקֶר שֶׁלְּמָחֳרָת = the following morning.

s.line: The little girl was quite frightened when she saw the great pile of shaggy wolves,
s.note: נִבְהַל (nif'al, active meaning) = to get a fright. A related word is בֶּהָלָה (panic). אַל תִּבָּהֵל = don't panic.

s.line: but the Tin Woodman told her all.
She thanked him for saving them and sat down to breakfast, after which they started again upon their journey.
s.note: הוֹדָה לְ־ … עַל = to thank someone for something; before a verb it is עַל שֶׁ: תּוֹדָה עַל שֶׁבָּאתָ (thanks for coming). יָצָא לַדֶּרֶךְ = to set out; דֶּרֶךְ צְלֵחָה! = have a good trip.

s.line: Now this same morning the Wicked Witch came to the door of her castle and looked out with her one eye that could see far off.
s.note: בְּאוֹתוֹ בֹּקֶר: before a noun, אוֹתוֹ means "the same" (אוֹתוֹ דָּבָר = the same thing). Elsewhere אוֹתוֹ is "him" (רָאִיתִי אוֹתוֹ). Same spelling, two jobs.

s.line: She saw all her wolves lying dead, and the strangers still traveling through her country.
s.note: עָשָׂה אֶת דַּרְכּוֹ = to make one's way: הוּא עוֹשֶׂה אֶת דַּרְכּוֹ הַבַּיְתָה (he's on his way home). זָר = a stranger or foreigner; שָׂפָה זָרָה = a foreign language.

s.line: This made her angrier than before, and she blew her silver whistle twice.
s.note: A pa'al / hif'il pair: כָּעַס = to be angry, הִכְעִיס = to make someone angry; זֶה מַכְעִיס אוֹתִי (that makes me angry). פַּעֲמַיִם = twice, a dual form of פַּעַם.

s.line: Straightway a great flock of wild crows came flying toward her, enough to darken the sky.
s.note: מַסְפִּיק = enough, the participle of הִסְפִּיק, which you saw above as "manage". It also means "stop it!": מַסְפִּיק!. לְעֶבְרָהּ = toward her (לְעֵבֶר + "her").

s.line: And the Wicked Witch said to the King Crow, “Fly at once to the strangers; peck out their eyes and tear them to pieces.”
s.note: נַקְּרוּ לָהֶם אֶת הָעֵינַיִם: with body parts Hebrew often marks the owner with לְ־ instead of a possessive: הוּא שָׁבַר לִי אֶת הַטֵּלֶפוֹן (he broke my phone). עוּפוּ, נַקְּרוּ and קִרְעוּ are plural imperatives, addressed to the whole flock.

s.line: The wild crows flew in one great flock toward Dorothy and her companions.
When the little girl saw them coming she was afraid.
But the Scarecrow said, “This is my battle, so lie down beside me and you will not be harmed.”
s.note: נִפְגַּע (nif'al) = to be hurt, the passive of פָּגַע בְּ־ (to hit, hurt). In the news נִפְגָּעִים are casualties, and אֵין נִפְגָּעִים means nobody was hurt. In speech נִפְגַּעְתִּי also means "I was offended".

s.line: So they all lay upon the ground except the Scarecrow, and he stood up and stretched out his arms.
s.note: פָּרַשׂ (with שׂ) = to spread out: פָּרַשׂ כְּנָפַיִם (spread its wings). Don't confuse it with פָּרַשׁ (with שׁ) = to retire, withdraw: הוּא פָּרַשׁ לַגִּמְלָאוֹת (he retired). Without the dot, both are פרש.

s.line: And when the crows saw him they were frightened, as these birds always are by scarecrows, and did not dare to come any nearer.
s.note: עוֹרֵב is masculine, but צִפּוֹר is feminine, so "the birds" take הָאֵלֶּה … נִבְהָלוֹת. הֵעֵז = to dare: אַל תָּעֵז! (don't you dare!). נִבְהַל מִ־ = to be frightened of.

s.line: But the King Crow said:
“It is only a stuffed man.
s.note: מְמֻלָּא (pu'al) = stuffed, filled, the passive of מִלֵּא (to fill). On an Israeli menu פִּלְפֵּל מְמֻלָּא is a stuffed pepper. מִלֵּא טֹפֶס = to fill in a form.

s.line: I will peck his eyes out.”
The King Crow flew at the Scarecrow, who caught it by the head and twisted its neck until it died.
s.note: הִתְנַפֵּל עַל = to pounce on, attack; also "to fall upon" food: הַיְּלָדִים הִתְנַפְּלוּ עַל הָעוּגָה. It is hitpa'el of נָפַל (to fall).

s.line: And then another crow flew at him, and the Scarecrow twisted its neck also.
There were forty crows, and forty times the Scarecrow twisted a neck, until at last all were lying dead beside him.
s.note: סוֹבֵב = to turn something around; its hitpa'el הִסְתּוֹבֵב = to turn yourself around, or to wander about: הִסְתּוֹבַבְנוּ בָּעִיר (we walked around town).

s.line: Then he called to his companions to rise, and again they went upon their journey.

w: יָצְאָה מִכֵּלֶיהָ|flew into a rage|~idiom: lit. went out of her vessels
s.line: When the Wicked Witch looked out again and saw all her crows lying in a heap, she got into a terrible rage, and blew three times upon her silver whistle.
s.note: יָצָא מִכֵּלָיו = to lose one's temper completely, still common in modern Hebrew: הַמְּאַמֵּן יָצָא מִכֵּלָיו (the coach blew his top). The suffix changes with the person: יָצְאָה מִכֵּלֶיהָ for "she". הֵצִיץ = to peek, take a quick look.

s.line: Forthwith there was heard a great buzzing in the air, and a swarm of black bees came flying toward her.
s.note: נִשְׁמַע (nif'al) = was heard, the passive of שָׁמַע. It also means "sounds": זֶה נִשְׁמָע טוֹב (that sounds good), and מָה נִשְׁמָע? is the everyday "how's it going?". תֵּכֶף וּמִיָּד = right away, at once.

s.line: “Go to the strangers and sting them to death!” commanded the Witch,
s.note: פָּקַד = to command, order; from the same root come פְּקֻדָּה (an order, and a computer command) and מְפַקֵּד (a commander). עָקַץ = to sting, and also to make a cutting remark: הֶעָרָה עוֹקֶצֶת.

s.line: and the bees turned and flew rapidly until they came to where Dorothy and her friends were walking.
But the Woodman had seen them coming, and the Scarecrow had decided what to do.
s.note: Hebrew has no pluperfect ("had seen"); the simple past with כְּבָר (already) does the job. דְּבוֹרָה is feminine, so the bees are אוֹתָן בָּאוֹת, not אוֹתָם בָּאִים.

s.line: “Take out my straw and scatter it over the little girl and the dog and the Lion,” he said to the Woodman, “and the bees cannot sting them.”
s.note: הוֹצִיא (hif'il) = to take out, "make go out", from יָצָא (to go out). It is also "to spend" money: הוֹצֵאתִי הַרְבֵּה כֶּסֶף. פִּזֵּר (pi'el) = to scatter, spread.

s.line: This the Woodman did,
and as Dorothy lay close beside the Lion and held Toto in her arms, the straw covered them entirely.
s.note: צָמוּד לְ־ = right up against, attached to; חֲנָיָה צְמוּדָה in a flat advert is a parking space that comes with the apartment. כֵּיוָן שֶׁ = since, because, a little more formal than כִּי.

w: חוּץ מֵאִישׁ הַפַּח|except the Tin Woodman
s.line: The bees came and found no one but the Woodman to sting,
so they flew at him and broke off all their stings against the tin, without hurting the Woodman at all.
s.note: פָּגַע בְּ־ = to hurt or hit someone; the object takes בְּ־, not אֶת. Its nif'al נִפְגַּע (was hurt) appeared a few paragraphs back. נִשְׁבַּר = broke, got broken; in speech נִשְׁבַּר לִי = I've had enough.

s.line: And as bees cannot live when their stings are broken that was the end of the black bees,
s.note: Two passives from one root: נִשְׁבַּר (nif'al) is the event, "got broken"; שָׁבוּר (pa'ul) is the resulting state, "broken". So הַכּוֹס נִשְׁבְּרָה (the glass broke), and now הַכּוֹס שְׁבוּרָה (the glass is broken).

s.line: and they lay scattered thick about the Woodman, like little heaps of fine coal.
s.note: A pi'el / pu'al pair: פִּזֵּר = to scatter (the Scarecrow's order above), מְפֻזָּר = scattered. Of a person, מְפֻזָּר means scatterbrained: הוּא קְצָת מְפֻזָּר.

w: טוֹב כְּמוֹ חָדָשׁ|as good as new|~idiom
s.line: Then Dorothy and the Lion got up, and the girl helped the Tin Woodman put the straw back into the Scarecrow again, until he was as good as ever.
s.note: עָזַר לְ־ = to help someone; the person helped takes לְ־: אֶפְשָׁר לַעֲזֹר לְךָ? (can I help you?), a phrase you will hear in every shop.

s.line: So they started upon their journey once more.
The Wicked Witch was so angry when she saw her black bees in little heaps like fine coal that she stamped her foot and tore her hair and gnashed her teeth.
s.note: כָּל כָּךְ … שֶׁ = "so … that". חָרַק שִׁנַּיִם = to grind one's teeth, and also to do something reluctantly: הוּא הִסְכִּים בַּחֲרִיקַת שִׁנַּיִם (he agreed through gritted teeth), a common news phrase.

s.line: And then she called a dozen of her slaves, who were the Winkies, and gave them sharp spears, telling them to go to the strangers and destroy them.
s.note: תְּרֵיסַר = a dozen: תְּרֵיסַר בֵּיצִים (a dozen eggs). קָרָא לְ־ = to call someone (to come), while קָרָא + אֶת = to read.

s.line: The Winkies were not a brave people, but they had to do as they were told.
s.note: אָמְרוּ לָהֶם = "they were told": a third-person plural verb with no subject is the usual everyday substitute for a passive. אוֹמְרִים שֶׁ… = they say that …, it is said that …. חַיָּב = must, obliged; it also means "owing": אַתָּה חַיָּב לִי כֶּסֶף.

s.line: So they marched away until they came near to Dorothy.
s.note: צָעַד = to march, to step; צַעַד = a step, also figuratively: צַעַד חָשׁוּב (an important step). צְעָדָה = a march or organized walk.

s.line: Then the Lion gave a great roar and sprang towards them,

w: כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מַהֵר|as fast as possible|~idiom
s.line: and the poor Winkies were so frightened that they ran back as fast as they could.
s.note: כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר + adverb = "as … as possible": כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מַהֵר (as fast as possible), כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מֻקְדָּם (as early as possible). Very common in speech and in emails.

s.line: When they returned to the castle the Wicked Witch beat them well with a strap, and sent them back to their work,
s.note: הִצְלִיף בְּ־ = to whip, lash; the person whipped takes בְּ־. It is also used of sharp criticism: הַשַּׂר הִצְלִיף בַּמְּמַשָּׁלָה. רְצוּעָה = a strap, a leash, and also a strip of land: רְצוּעַת חוֹף (a coastal strip).

s.line: after which she sat down to think what she should do next.
s.note: הָלְאָה = onward, further on: וְכֵן הָלְאָה = and so on (written וכו׳), בּוֹא נַמְשִׁיךְ הָלְאָה = let's move on.

s.line: She could not understand how all her plans to destroy these strangers had failed;
s.note: נִכְשַׁל (nif'al, active meaning) = to fail: נִכְשַׁלְתִּי בַּמִּבְחָן (I failed the exam). כִּשָּׁלוֹן = a failure. Note the spelling תָּכְנִית: the first vowel is a short o (kamatz katan), "tokhnit".

s.line: but she was a powerful Witch, as well as a wicked one, and she soon made up her mind how to act.

w: וְאַבְנֵי אֹדֶם|and rubies|~lit. stones of red
s.line: There was, in her cupboard, a Golden Cap, with a circle of diamonds and rubies running round it.
s.note: אֹדֶם = ruby (the stone), and also lipstick (שְׂפָתוֹן is the more common word for that), from the root of אָדֹם (red). טַבַּעַת = a ring, here a circle of stones; טַבַּעַת נִשּׂוּאִין = a wedding ring.

s.line: This Golden Cap had a charm.
Whoever owned it could call three times upon the Winged Monkeys, who would obey any order they were given.
s.note: הָיוּ מְמַלְּאִים: הָיָה + participle describes what would happen or used to happen. מִלֵּא פְּקֻדָּה = to carry out an order. נִתַּן (nif'al) = was given, the passive of נָתַן. זִמֵּן = to summon; זִמּוּן = a summons, for example to court.

s.line: But no person could command these strange creatures more than three times.
s.note: פִּקֵּד עַל (pi'el) = to be in command of, while פָּקַד (pa'al), used earlier in this chapter, = to give an order. יְצוּר = a creature, related to יָצַר (to create).

s.line: Twice already the Wicked Witch had used the charm of the Cap.
s.note: הִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּ־ = to use; the thing used takes בְּ־: אֶפְשָׁר לְהִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בַּטֵּלֶפוֹן שֶׁלְּךָ?. With a root starting in שׁ, the ת of hitpa'el again swaps places: הִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ, not *הִתְשַׁמֵּשׁ.

s.line: Once was when she had made the Winkies her slaves, and set herself to rule over their country.
s.note: הִשְׁתַּלֵּט עַל = to take control of, seize; a news word (הַצָּבָא הִשְׁתַּלֵּט עַל הָעִיר), and also everyday: הַחֲתוּל הִשְׁתַּלֵּט עַל הַסַּפָּה. Related: שִׁלְטוֹן (rule, regime), שֶׁלֶט (a sign) and שַׁלָּט (a remote control).

s.line: The Winged Monkeys had helped her do this.
The second time was when she had fought against the Great Oz himself, and driven him out of the land of the West.
s.note: נִלְחַם (nif'al, active meaning) = to fight; מִלְחָמָה (war) shares the root. גֵּרֵשׁ (pi'el) = to expel, drive out, and in speech, to kick out: גֵּרְשׁוּ אוֹתוֹ מֵהַכִּתָּה (he was sent out of class). הִתְגָּרֵשׁ = to get divorced.

s.line: The Winged Monkeys had also helped her in doing this.
Only once more could she use this Golden Cap,
for which reason she did not like to do so until all her other powers were exhausted.
s.note: נִגְמַר (nif'al) = ran out, ended: נִגְמַר לִי הַכֶּסֶף (I've run out of money), נִגְמַר הֶחָלָב (the milk is finished). כָּל עוֹד = as long as; כָּל עוֹד לֹא = as long as … not, i.e. until.

s.line: But now that her fierce wolves and her wild crows and her stinging bees were gone, and her slaves had been scared away by the Cowardly Lion,
s.note: English "had been scared away by the Lion" becomes active Hebrew, with the object first for emphasis: אֶת הָעֲבָדִים שֶׁלָּהּ הִבְרִיחַ הָאַרְיֵה. הִבְרִיחַ (hif'il) = to make someone flee, from בָּרַח (to flee). It also means "to smuggle": הַבְרָחַת סַמִּים (drug smuggling).

s.line: she saw there was only one way left to destroy Dorothy and her friends.
So the Wicked Witch took the Golden Cap from her cupboard and placed it upon her head.
s.note: Hebrew has a different "put on" verb for each item: חָבַשׁ a hat or helmet, לָבַשׁ clothes, נָעַל shoes, הִרְכִּיב glasses. חָבַשׁ also means to bandage: חוֹבֵשׁ = an army medic.

s.line: Then she stood upon her left foot and said, slowly:
s.note: רֶגֶל שְׂמֹאל, יַד יָמִין: Hebrew often puts the plain words שְׂמֹאל / יָמִין after the noun instead of an adjective. יַד יָמִין is also someone's "right-hand man".

s.line: “Ep-pe, pep-pe, kak-ke!”
s.note: The magic words are Baum's own nonsense, so they are simply written in Hebrew letters.

s.line: Next she stood upon her right foot and said:
“Hil-lo, hol-lo, hel-lo!”

w: בְּקוֹל רָם|in a loud voice|~idiom: aloud
s.line: After this she stood upon both feet and cried in a loud voice:
s.note: בְּקוֹל רָם = aloud, in a loud voice: תִּקְרָא אֶת זֶה בְּקוֹל רָם (read it aloud). שְׁתֵּי is "two" before a feminine noun; רֶגֶל is feminine.

s.line: “Ziz-zy, zuz-zy, zik!”
Now the charm began to work.
s.note: פָּעַל = to work, function, operate (a machine, a charm, a plan); לַעֲבֹד is for people doing work, though in speech זֶה לֹא עוֹבֵד is also heard. פָּעַל also means "to act": צָרִיךְ לִפְעֹל מַהֵר.

s.line: The sky was darkened, and a low rumbling sound was heard in the air.
s.note: הֶחְשִׁיךְ works both ways: earlier the crows הֶחְשִׁיכוּ אֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם (darkened the sky), and here the sky itself הֶחְשִׁיךְ (grew dark). הַשָּׁמַיִם is plural in Hebrew, so the verb is plural too.

s.line: There was a rushing of many wings, a great chattering and laughing,
s.note: מַשַּׁק כְּנָפַיִם = the beating of wings, a fixed phrase in Hebrew writing. פִּטְפּוּט = chatter; פִּטְפֵּט (to chatter) is one of the many Hebrew verbs that repeat their consonants.

s.line: and the sun came out of the dark sky to show the Wicked Witch surrounded by a crowd of monkeys, each with a pair of immense and powerful wings on his shoulders.
s.note: A hif'il / hof'al pair: הִקִּיף = to surround, מֻקָּף = surrounded (fem. מֻקֶּפֶת). מַקִּיף = comprehensive: בִּטּוּחַ מַקִּיף is comprehensive car insurance. כָּנָף is feminine, so the wings are עֲנָקִיּוֹת וַחֲזָקוֹת.

s.line: One, much bigger than the others, seemed to be their leader.
He flew close to the Witch and said, “You have called us for the third and last time.
s.note: קָרָאת = you (fem.) called; the א of the root stays silent before the ending ת. בַּפַּעַם הָאַחֲרוֹנָה = for the last time; בַּפַּעַם הַבָּאָה = next time.

s.line: What do you command?”
s.note: צִוָּה (pi'el) = to command, order, a formal word. מִצְוָה (a commandment; a good deed) shares the root.

s.line: “Go to the strangers who are within my land and destroy them all except the Lion,” said the Wicked Witch.
s.note: נִמְצָא (nif'al ptc) = is located, is (somewhere): אֵיפֹה נִמְצָא הַבַּנְק? (where is the bank?). Literally it is "is found". חוּץ מִ־ = except, apart from.

w: בָּא לִי|I feel like|~idiom: lit. it comes to me
s.line: “Bring that beast to me, for I have a mind to harness him like a horse, and make him work.”
s.note: בָּא לִי = I feel like, I'm in the mood for, very common in speech: בָּא לִי גְּלִידָה, לֹא בָּא לִי לָלֶכֶת. רָתַם = to harness, also figuratively: לִרְתֹּם אֶת הַצִּבּוּר (to enlist the public). הֶעֱבִיד = to make someone work, the hif'il of עָבַד.

s.line: “Your commands shall be obeyed,” said the leader.
s.note: יְבֻצְּעוּ is a pu'al future, the passive of בִּצֵּעַ (to carry out, perform): הָעֲבוֹדוֹת יְבֻצְּעוּ בַּלַּיְלָה (the works will be carried out at night), typical of official notices. מִבְצָע = a sale or special offer in a shop, and also a military operation.

s.line: Then, with a great deal of chattering and noise, the Winged Monkeys flew away to the place where Dorothy and her friends were walking.
Some of the Monkeys seized the Tin Woodman and carried him through the air until they were over a country thickly covered with sharp rocks.
s.note: חֵלֶק מֵהַקּוֹפִים תָּפְסוּ: חֵלֶק ("part") is singular, but when it means "some of" a group, the verb usually goes in the plural, agreeing with the people (or monkeys) meant. מְכֻסֶּה is the pu'al participle of כִּסָּה (to cover): הַשֻּׁלְחָן מְכֻסֶּה בְּמַפָּה = the table is covered with a tablecloth.

s.line: Here they dropped the poor Woodman,
s.note: הִפִּיל (hif'il) = to drop, make fall; it is the causative of נָפַל (to fall), which comes in the very next sentence. You'll hear הִפַּלְתִּי אֶת הַטֵּלֵפוֹן = I dropped my phone.

s.line: who fell a great distance to the rocks,
where he lay so battered and dented that he could neither move nor groan.
s.note: לֹא… וְלֹא… = "neither … nor …": לֹא קָפֶה וְלֹא תֵּה (neither coffee nor tea). לָזוּז (to move, budge) is very common: אַל תָּזוּז! = don't move! תָּזוּז! = move over!

s.line: Others of the Monkeys caught the Scarecrow,
and with their long fingers pulled all of the straw out of his clothes and head.
s.note: שָׁלַף = to pull out, draw out (a sword, a card, a gun). You'll also hear it of a quick answer: הוּא שָׁלַף תְּשׁוּבָה = he shot back an answer on the spot.

s.line: They made his hat and boots and clothes into a small bundle and threw it into the top branches of a tall tree.
The remaining Monkeys threw pieces of stout rope around the Lion and wound many coils about his body and head and legs,
s.note: שְׁאָר + noun = "the rest of": שְׁאָר הַקּוֹפִים, שְׁאָר הַיּוֹם (the rest of the day). The fixed phrase בֵּין הַשְּׁאָר = among other things.

s.line: until he was unable to bite or scratch or struggle in any way.
s.note: מְסֻגָּל לְ־ = capable of, able to; in form a pu'al participle. It is a little stronger than יָכוֹל: הוּא לֹא מְסֻגָּל לְשַׁקֵּר = he is incapable of lying. לְהֵאָבֵק (nif'al, active meaning) = to struggle, wrestle; the noun מַאֲבָק (struggle, fight) is everywhere in the news.

s.line: Then they lifted him up and flew away with him to the Witch’s castle,
where he was placed in a small yard with a high iron fence around it, so that he could not escape.
s.note: Two hof'al passives: הוּשַׂם (was put) is the passive of שָׂם (to put), and מֻקָּף (surrounded) is the passive participle of hif'il הִקִּיף (to surround). מֻקָּף is common in descriptions: בַּיִת מֻקָּף גִּנָּה = a house surrounded by a garden. Note that חָצֵר (yard) is feminine: קְטַנָּה, שֶׁהָיְתָה.

s.line: But Dorothy they did not harm at all.
s.note: פָּגַע בְּ־ = to harm, hurt, hit; the object takes בְּ־, so the fronted object is בְּדוֹרוֹתִי. It also means to offend: לֹא הִתְכַּוַּנְתִּי לִפְגֹּעַ בְּךָ = I didn't mean to hurt your feelings. Putting the object first, as Baum does, works in Hebrew too and stresses it.

s.line: She stood, with Toto in her arms, watching the sad fate of her comrades and thinking it would soon be her turn.
s.note: הַתּוֹר שֶׁלָּהּ = her turn. תּוֹר is also a queue or an appointment: לַעֲמֹד בַּתּוֹר (to stand in line), לִקְבֹּעַ תּוֹר לָרוֹפֵא (to book a doctor's appointment), and מִי בַּתּוֹר? = who's next?

s.line: The leader of the Winged Monkeys flew up to her, his long, hairy arms stretched out and his ugly face grinning terribly;
s.note: כְּשֶׁ + a clause with no verb is the Hebrew way to say "with his arms stretched out": כְּשֶׁהַזְּרוֹעוֹת שֶׁלּוֹ פְּרוּשׂוֹת. פָּנִים (face) is plural in form, so its adjectives and verbs are plural too: הַפָּנִים הַמְּכֹעָרִים שֶׁלּוֹ מְחַיְּכִים. מְחַיְּכִים חִיּוּךְ is the verb + noun of the same root you already know.

s.line: but he saw the mark of the Good Witch’s kiss upon her forehead and stopped short,
s.note: נֶעֱצַר (nif'al) = came to a stop; the pa'al עָצַר = to stop something, and also to arrest: הַמִּשְׁטָרָה עָצְרָה שְׁנֵי חֲשׁוּדִים (police arrested two suspects). בְּבַת אַחַת = all at once, suddenly.

s.line: motioning the others not to touch her.
s.note: סִמֵּן (pi'el) = to signal, gesture, or mark; it comes from the same root as סִימָן (mark, sign) in the sentence before. נָגַע בְּ־ takes בְּ־: אַל תִּגַּע בָּזֶה! = don't touch that!

s.line: “We dare not harm this little girl,” he said to them,
s.note: הֵעֵז (hif'il) = to dare: אֵיךְ אַתָּה מֵעֵז? = how dare you? The adjective נוֹעָז = daring, bold.

w: מִכֹּחַ הָרַע|than the Power of Evil
s.line: “for she is protected by the Power of Good, and that is greater than the Power of Evil.
s.note: עַל יְדֵי (literally "by the hands of") introduces who does the action in a passive sentence, like English "by". מוּגָן (protected) is the hof'al of הֵגֵן (to protect); compare מָגֵן (shield) and מָגֵן דָּוִד.

s.line: All we can do is to carry her to the castle of the Wicked Witch and leave her there.”
s.note: לְהַשְׁאִיר (hif'il) = to leave something somewhere; it is the causative of נִשְׁאַר (to stay, remain): תַּשְׁאִיר לִי הוֹדָעָה = leave me a message.

s.line: So, carefully and gently, they lifted Dorothy in their arms and carried her swiftly through the air until they came to the castle,
s.note: בְּ־ + an abstract noun makes an adverb: בִּזְהִירוּת (with care = carefully), בַּעֲדִינוּת (gently), בִּמְהִירוּת (quickly). The road sign סַע בִּזְהִירוּת = drive carefully.

s.line: where they set her down upon the front doorstep.
Then the leader said to the Witch:
“We have obeyed you as far as we were able.
s.note: צִיֵּת לְ־ (pi'el) = to obey, with לְ־: הוּא לֹא מְצַיֵּת לַחֻקִּים = he doesn't obey the rules. כְּכָל שֶׁ = "as far as / as much as", slightly formal: כְּכָל שֶׁיָּדוּעַ לִי = as far as I know.

s.line: The Tin Woodman and the Scarecrow are destroyed, and the Lion is tied up in your yard.
s.note: הֻשְׁמְדוּ = were destroyed, the hof'al (passive) of הִשְׁמִיד (to destroy). The noun הַשְׁמָדָה (destruction) is news vocabulary. קָשׁוּר (tied) is a pa'ul participle and also means "connected": זֶה לֹא קָשׁוּר = that's not related.

s.line: The little girl we dare not harm, nor the dog she carries in her arms.
Your power over our band is now ended, and you will never see us again.”
s.note: הִסְתַּיֵּם (hitpa'el) = to come to an end; its active partner is pi'el סִיֵּם (to finish), as in סִיַּמְתִּי = I'm done. לְעוֹלָם לֹא = never, used mostly about the future; אַף פַּעַם לֹא works for any tense.

w: מִן הָעַיִן|from sight|~lit. from the eye
s.line: Then all the Winged Monkeys, with much laughing and chattering and noise, flew into the air and were soon out of sight.
s.note: תּוֹךְ + noun = "amid, while …ing": תּוֹךְ צְחוֹק (while laughing), תּוֹךְ כְּדֵי הֲלִיכָה (while walking). עַד מְהֵרָה = soon, before long, a bookish but still common phrase. נֶעֱלַם (nif'al, active meaning) = to disappear.

s.line: The Wicked Witch was both surprised and worried when she saw the mark on Dorothy’s forehead,
s.note: גַּם… וְגַם… = "both … and …". הֻפְתְּעָה is the hof'al (passive) of hif'il הִפְתִּיעַ (to surprise); compare הַפְתָּעָה (a surprise) and מַפְתִּיעַ (surprising).

s.line: for she knew well that neither the Winged Monkeys nor she, herself, dare hurt the girl in any way.
s.note: הִיא עַצְמָהּ = she herself. עֶצֶם + a possessive ending gives "-self": עַצְמִי (myself), עַצְמוֹ (himself). The verb is masculine plural because the subjects are mixed. בְּשׁוּם צוּרָה = in no way, by no means.

s.line: She looked down at Dorothy’s feet,
s.note: הִשְׁפִּיל מַבָּט = to lower one's eyes, look down; הִשְׁפִּיל (hif'il, from שָׁפֵל low) also means "to humiliate", and הַשְׁפָּלָה = humiliation.

s.line: and seeing the Silver Shoes, began to tremble with fear, for she knew what a powerful charm belonged to them.
s.note: בָּהֶן (in them, feminine) because נַעֲלַיִם is feminine. מִפַּחַד: מִ־ gives the cause, "from / out of": רָעַד מִקֹּר (shivered with cold), מֵת מִצְּחוֹק (died laughing).

s.line: At first the Witch was tempted to run away from Dorothy;
s.note: הִתְפַּתָּה (hitpa'el) = to be tempted, to give in to temptation; the pi'el פִּתָּה = to tempt, and פִּתּוּי = temptation. Hebrew uses an active-looking reflexive verb where English says "was tempted".

s.line: but she happened to look into the child’s eyes and saw how simple the soul behind them was,
s.note: הִסְתַּכֵּל לְמִישֶׁהוּ בָּעֵינַיִם = to look someone in the eye; Hebrew marks the person with לְ־ and the body part with the definite article, not "his eyes": תִּסְתַּכֵּל לִי בָּעֵינַיִם. בְּמִקְרֶה = by chance, and בְּמִקְרֶה? on its own = "by any chance?". תָּמִים = innocent, naive.

s.line: and that the little girl did not know of the wonderful power the Silver Shoes gave her.
s.note: After "saw that" or "knew that", Hebrew keeps the tense of the original thought: <t>לֹא יוֹדַעַת</t> and <t>נוֹתְנוֹת</t> are present, where English shifts to "did not know" and "gave". <t>אָמַר שֶׁהוּא עָיֵף</t> = he said he was tired.

s.line: So the Wicked Witch laughed to herself, and thought,
“I can still make her my slave, for she does not know how to use her power.”
s.note: הָפַךְ … לְ־ = to turn something into: הָפַךְ אֶת הַחֶדֶר לְמִשְׂרָד. Without לְ־ it means to turn over: הָפַךְ אֶת הַדַּף. הִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּ־ = to use, with בְּ־.

s.line: Then she said to Dorothy, harshly and severely:
s.note: חָמוּר = severe, serious: מַצָּב חָמוּר (a serious situation), פְּצִיעָה חֲמוּרָה (a serious injury). The same letters spell חֲמוֹר (donkey).

s.line: “Come with me;

w: וְשֶׁתְּצַיְּתִי|and see that you obey|pi'el · צ־י־ת
s.line: and see that you mind everything I tell you, for if you do not I will make an end of you, as I did of the Tin Woodman and the Scarecrow.”
s.note: שֶׁתְּצַיְּתִי: שֶׁ + future, with no main verb, is a firm command or warning: שֶׁלֹּא תָּעֵז! = don't you dare! חִסֵּל (pi'el) = to wipe out, eliminate; in the news חִסּוּל means a targeted killing, and in everyday talk חִסַּלְנוּ אֶת הָעוּגָה = we polished off the cake.

s.line: Dorothy followed her through many of the beautiful rooms in her castle until they came to the kitchen,
where the Witch bade her clean the pots and kettles and sweep the floor and keep the fire fed with wood.
s.note: צִוָּה עַל + person + infinitive = to order someone to do something; the noun is צַו (order, decree) and מִצְוָה (commandment). הֵזִין (hif'il) = to feed, nourish; תְּזוּנָה = nutrition, and in computing לְהַזִּין סִסְמָה = to enter a password.

s.line: Dorothy went to work meekly, with her mind made up to work as hard as she could;
s.note: נִגַּשׁ לַעֲבוֹדָה = to set to work, get down to work; נִגַּשׁ (nif'al, active meaning) is literally "to approach": נִגַּשְׁתִּי לַבְּחִינָה = I sat the exam. כְּכָל שֶׁתּוּכַל = as much as she could; the future תּוּכַל is used here, though English says "could".

s.line: for she was glad the Wicked Witch had decided not to kill her.
With Dorothy hard at work, the Witch thought she would go into the courtyard and harness the Cowardly Lion like a horse;
s.note: רָתַם = to harness an animal. It is common in a figurative sense: לִרְתֹּם אֶת הַצִּבּוּר לַמַּאֲמָץ = to enlist the public in the effort.

s.line: it would amuse her, she was sure, to make him draw her chariot whenever she wished to go to drive.
s.note: שִׁעֲשֵׁעַ = to amuse; שַׁעֲשׁוּעַ = amusement, and מְשַׁעֲשֵׁעַ = amusing. הִכְרִיחַ (hif'il) = to force, compel; מֻכְרָח = forced, "must": אֲנִי מֻכְרָח לָלֶכֶת = I have to go. לָצֵאת לְסִבּוּב = to go out for a ride or a spin.

s.line: But as she opened the gate the Lion gave a loud roar and bounded at her so fiercely that the Witch was afraid,
s.note: זִנֵּק עַל (pi'el) = to leap at, pounce on; זִנּוּק is also the start of a race and a sharp jump in prices: זִנּוּק בַּמְּחִירִים. נִבְהַל (nif'al) = to get a fright: אַל תִּבָּהֵל = don't be alarmed.

s.line: and ran out and shut the gate again.
s.note: יָצְאָה בְּרִיצָה = "went out at a run", i.e. ran out. Hebrew often joins a verb of motion with בְּ־ + a noun of manner: נִכְנַס בְּרִיצָה (ran in), יָצָא בִּסְעָרָה (stormed out).

s.line: “If I cannot harness you,” said the Witch to the Lion, speaking through the bars of the gate,
s.note: מִבַּעַד לְ־ = through (a window, bars, a veil), a literary but well-known preposition. סוֹרְגִים = bars; the idiom מֵאֲחוֹרֵי סוֹרָג וּבְרִיחַ = behind bars, in prison.

s.line: “I can starve you.
s.note: הִרְעִיב (hif'il) = to starve someone, make him hungry: the causative of רָעֵב (hungry). אֲנִי מֵת מֵרָעָב = I'm starving (lit. dying of hunger).

s.line: You shall have nothing to eat until you do as I wish.”
So after that she took no food to the imprisoned Lion;
s.note: כָּלוּא = locked up, imprisoned, a pa'ul participle; כֶּלֶא = prison. מֵאָז = since then, from then on: מֵאָז הוּא לֹא חָזַר = he hasn't come back since.

s.line: but every day she came to the gate at noon and asked,
s.note: הָיְתָה בָּאָה… וְשׁוֹאֶלֶת: הָיָה + participle describes a repeated habit in the past, like English "would" or "used to": בַּקַּיִץ הָיִינוּ הוֹלְכִים לַיָּם = in summer we used to go to the beach.

s.line: “Are you ready to be harnessed like a horse?”
s.note: לְהֵרָתֵם is the nif'al infinitive, the passive of לִרְתֹּם (to harness): pa'al רָתַם harnessed → nif'al נִרְתַּם was harnessed. It is also used for "to pitch in, get on board": כֻּלָּם נִרְתְּמוּ לָעֶזְרָה = everyone pitched in to help.

s.line: And the Lion would answer,
“No.
If you come in this yard, I will bite you.”
s.note: After אִם (if) about the future, Hebrew uses the future in both halves: אִם תִּכָּנְסִי… אֶנְשֹׁךְ, where English has "if you come in… I will bite". נִכְנַס is nif'al with an active meaning, "to enter".

s.line: The reason the Lion did not have to do as the Witch wished was that every night, while the woman was asleep, Dorothy carried him food from the cupboard.
s.note: הַסִּבָּה… הָיְתָה שֶׁ… = "the reason … was that …". The verb הָיְתָה is feminine to agree with סִבָּה, even though it comes many words later. In speech you'll hear הַסִּבָּה הִיא שֶׁ… = the reason is that…

s.line: After he had eaten he would lie down on his bed of straw,
and Dorothy would lie beside him and put her head on his soft, shaggy mane,
s.note: פָּרוּעַ = wild, unkempt (of hair), a pa'ul participle: שֵׂעָר פָּרוּעַ = messy hair. It also describes lawlessness: הַמַּעֲרָב הַפָּרוּעַ = the Wild West. לְיָדוֹ = next to him, from לְיַד.

s.line: while they talked of their troubles and tried to plan some way to escape.
s.note: צָרוֹת = troubles; צָרָה is the everyday word for a problem or misfortune, as in אֵין לִי מַסְפִּיק צָרוֹת? = don't I have enough problems?

s.line: But they could find no way to get out of the castle,
for it was constantly guarded by the yellow Winkies,
s.note: שָׁמוּר (pa'ul of שָׁמַר) = guarded, kept, reserved: כָּל הַזְּכֻיּוֹת שְׁמוּרוֹת = all rights reserved, מָקוֹם שָׁמוּר = a reserved seat. הִיא refers to the castle, because טִירָה is feminine.

s.line: who were the slaves of the Wicked Witch and too afraid of her not to do as she told them.
s.note: פָּחַד מִ־ = to be afraid of, with מִ־: מִמֶּנָּה = of her. English "too afraid of her not to do" is turned around into "so afraid that they always did", which is the more natural Hebrew order.

s.line: The girl had to work hard during the day,

w: וּלְעִתִּים קְרוֹבוֹת|and often|~lit. at near times
s.line: and often the Witch threatened to beat her with the same old umbrella she always carried in her hand.
s.note: אוֹתָהּ appears twice here with two meanings: לְהַכּוֹת אוֹתָהּ = to hit her (object marker), and בְּאוֹתָהּ מִטְרִיָּה = with the same umbrella. Before a noun, אוֹתוֹ / אוֹתָהּ / אוֹתָם means "the same". אִיֵּם (pi'el) = to threaten; אִיּוּם (a threat) is a news word.

s.line: But, in truth, she did not dare to strike Dorothy, because of the mark upon her forehead.
The child did not know this, and was full of fear for herself and Toto.
s.note: חָשַׁשׁ changes meaning with its preposition: חָשַׁשׁ מִ־ = to fear something (חָשַׁשְׁתִּי מִזֶּה = I was afraid of that), but חָשַׁשׁ לְ־ = to fear for someone: הוּא חָשַׁשׁ לְחַיָּיו = he feared for his life.

s.line: Once the Witch struck Toto a blow with her umbrella and the brave little dog flew at her and bit her leg in return.
s.note: הִסְתָּעֵר עַל = to charge at, storm; in hitpa'el the ת swaps places with a first root letter ס, so it is not הִתְסַעֵר. נָשַׁךְ אוֹתָהּ בָּרֶגֶל = "bit her in the leg": Hebrew names the person as the object and the body part with בְּ־.

s.line: The Witch did not bleed where she was bitten,
s.note: נִנְשְׁכָה = she was bitten, the nif'al (passive) of pa'al נָשַׁךְ from the sentence before. דִּמֵּם (pi'el) = to bleed, from דָּם (blood); דִּמּוּם = bleeding.

s.line: for she was so wicked that the blood in her had dried up many years before.
Dorothy’s life became very sad as she grew to understand that it would be harder than ever to get back to Kansas and Aunt Em again.
s.note: חַיִּים (life) is plural in Hebrew, so it takes נַעֲשׂוּ and עֲצוּבִים. נַעֲשָׂה (nif'al of עָשָׂה) = to become; it can also mean "was done": מָה נַעֲשָׂה? = what's been done? / what shall we do? מִתָּמִיד = than ever: יוֹתֵר טוֹב מִתָּמִיד = better than ever.

w: בְּמַר לִבָּהּ|bitterly|~idiom: in the bitterness of her heart
s.line: Sometimes she would cry bitterly for hours,
s.note: בָּכָה בְּמַר לִבּוֹ = to weep bitterly, a set phrase from מַר (bitter). הָיְתָה בּוֹכָה is the past habitual: "she would cry".

w: צַר לוֹ|he was sorry|~idiom: it is narrow to him
s.line: with Toto sitting at her feet and looking into her face, whining dismally to show how sorry he was for his little mistress.
s.note: צַר לִי = I'm sorry (lit. "it is narrow / tight for me"), a polite, slightly formal way to express regret: צַר לִי לִשְׁמֹעַ = I'm sorry to hear that. Everyday speech also says סְלִיחָה or אֲנִי מִצְטַעֵר. יִלֵּל = to whine or howl, like a dog or the wind.

w: הָיָה אִכְפַּת|it mattered|~idiom: (to X) it was of concern
בְּאֶרֶץ אוֹז|in the Land of Oz
s.line: Toto did not really care whether he was in Kansas or the Land of Oz so long as Dorothy was with him;
s.note: אִכְפַּת לְ־ = "to care", built like "having": the person who cares gets לְ־: לֹא אִכְפַּת לִי = I don't care, אִכְפַּת לְךָ? = do you mind? כָּל עוֹד = as long as.

s.line: but he knew the little girl was unhappy, and that made him unhappy too.
s.note: גָּרַם לְ־ + infinitive = to cause someone to, make someone: זֶה גָּרַם לִי לַחְשֹׁב = it made me think. מְאֻשָּׁר, the pu'al participle you know, here in its feminine form מְאֻשֶּׁרֶת.

s.line: Now the Wicked Witch had a great longing to have for her own the Silver Shoes which the girl always wore.
s.note: נָעַל has two meanings: to put on or wear shoes (נַעַל), and to lock (מַנְעוּל = a lock): נָעַלְתִּי אֶת הַדֶּלֶת = I locked the door. רָצָה שֶׁ + future = "wanted (something) to be": אֲנִי רוֹצֶה שֶׁתָּבוֹא = I want you to come.

s.line: Her bees and her crows and her wolves were lying in heaps and drying up,
s.note: עֲרֵמָה = a heap, pile: עֲרֵמַת כְּבִיסָה = a pile of laundry, and עֲרֵמוֹת שֶׁל = loads of.

s.line: and she had used up all the power of the Golden Cap;
s.note: נִצֵּל (pi'el) = to use, make use of, and also to exploit: לְנַצֵּל אֶת הַזְּמַן (to make good use of the time), הוּא נִצֵּל אוֹתִי (he took advantage of me). Without vowels it looks just like nif'al נִצַּל = was saved, rescued.

w: לָשִׂים יָד עַל|to get hold of|~idiom: to put a hand on
s.line: but if she could only get hold of the Silver Shoes,
s.note: For an imagined "if", Hebrew uses הָיָה + participle in both halves: אִם הָיְתָה מַצְלִיחָה… הֵן הָיוּ נוֹתְנוֹת = if she managed… they would give. לָשִׂים יָד עַל = to lay hands on, get hold of.

s.line: they would give her more power than all the other things she had lost.
s.note: אִבֵּד (pi'el) = to lose something; אָבַד (pa'al) = to be lost, get lost: אִבַּדְתִּי אֶת הַמַּפְתְּחוֹת = I lost the keys, but הַמַּפְתְּחוֹת אָבְדוּ = the keys are lost.

s.line: She watched Dorothy carefully, to see if she ever took off her shoes,
s.note: עָקַב אַחֲרֵי = to follow, track, keep watch on; מַעֲקָב = surveillance, follow-up, and on social media עוֹקְבִים = followers. חָלַץ = to take off shoes; it also means to rescue, and חִלּוּץ = rescue (from rubble).

s.line: thinking she might steal them.
But the child was so proud of her pretty shoes that she never took them off except at night and when she took her bath.
s.note: גֵּאֶה בְּ־ = proud of, with בְּ־: אֲנִי גֵּאָה בָּךְ = I'm proud of you. הִתְרַחֵץ (hitpa'el, "to wash oneself") = to bathe; compare רָחַץ (to wash something) and מִקְלַחַת (shower).

s.line: The Witch was too much afraid of the dark to dare go in Dorothy’s room at night to take the shoes,
s.note: יוֹתֵר מִדַּי… מִכְּדֵי + infinitive = "too … to …": הוּא עָיֵף מִדַּי מִכְּדֵי לִנְהֹג = he is too tired to drive. יוֹתֵר מִדַּי alone = too much.

s.line: and her dread of water was greater than her fear of the dark,
so she never came near when Dorothy was bathing.
s.note: הִתְקָרֵב (hitpa'el) = to come closer, approach, from קָרוֹב (near): אַל תִּתְקָרֵב! = keep away! / don't come any closer!

s.line: Indeed, the old Witch never touched water, nor ever let water touch her in any way.
s.note: נָתַן לְ־ + infinitive = to let, allow: תֵּן לִי לַעֲזֹר = let me help, הֵם לֹא נָתְנוּ לָנוּ לְהִכָּנֵס = they didn't let us in. לְמַעֲשֶׂה = in fact, actually.

s.line: But the wicked creature was very cunning,
s.note: מִרְשַׁעַת = a wicked woman, from רָשָׁע (wicked); today it is said half-jokingly of a mean woman. עַרְמוּמִי = sly, cunning; a fox in fables is הַשּׁוּעָל הָעַרְמוּמִי.

s.line: and she finally thought of a trick that would give her what she wanted.
s.note: תַּכְסִיס = a trick, ploy, tactic; in politics תַּכְסִיסִים = maneuvering, and תַּכְסִיס מַשְׁהֶה = a delaying tactic.

s.line: She placed a bar of iron in the middle of the kitchen floor,
and then by her magic arts made the iron invisible to human eyes.
s.note: בִּלְתִּי + participle or adjective = "un-, in-": בִּלְתִּי נִרְאֶה (invisible), בִּלְתִּי אֶפְשָׁרִי (impossible), בִּלְתִּי נִשְׁכָּח (unforgettable).

s.line: So that when Dorothy walked across the floor she stumbled over the bar, not being able to see it,
s.note: נִתְקַל בְּ־ (nif'al) = to trip over, and very often "to run into, come across": נִתְקַלְנוּ בִּבְעָיָה = we ran into a problem, נִתְקַלְתִּי בּוֹ בָּרְחוֹב = I bumped into him in the street.

w: מְלוֹא קוֹמָתָהּ|at full length|~idiom: the full measure of her height
s.line: and fell at full length.
She was not much hurt, but in her fall one of the Silver Shoes came off;
s.note: נִפְגַּע = was hurt, the nif'al (passive) of פָּגַע בְּ־ (to harm). News reports use it all the time: שְׁנַיִם נִפְגְּעוּ קָשׁוֹת = two were seriously injured, and נִפְגָּע = a casualty. It also means "offended": הִיא נִפְגְּעָה = her feelings were hurt.

s.line: and before she could reach it, the Witch had snatched it away and put it on her own skinny foot.
s.note: הִסְפִּיק (hif'il) = to manage (in time), get around to: לֹא הִסְפַּקְתִּי לֶאֱכֹל = I didn't have time to eat. It also means "to be enough": זֶה מַסְפִּיק = that's enough. חָטַף = to snatch, grab, and also to kidnap.

s.line: The wicked woman was greatly pleased with the success of her trick,
s.note: מְרֻצֶּה מִ־ = satisfied with, pleased with: the pu'al participle of רִצָּה (to please, satisfy). לָקוֹחוֹת מְרֻצִּים = satisfied customers; אֲנִי לֹא מְרֻצֶּה = I'm not happy with it.

w: הָיְתָה לָהּ|she had|~lit. there was to her
s.line: for as long as she had one of the shoes she owned half the power of their charm,
s.note: שַׁיָּךְ לְ־ = belongs to: לְמִי זֶה שַׁיָּךְ? = whose is this? It also means "relevant": זֶה לֹא שַׁיָּךְ = that's beside the point.

s.line: and Dorothy could not use it against her, even had she known how to do so.
s.note: אִלּוּ = "if" for something contrary to fact (she did not know how): אִלּוּ יָדַעְתִּי, הָיִיתִי בָּא = had I known, I would have come. For a real possibility Hebrew uses אִם.

s.line: The little girl, seeing she had lost one of her pretty shoes, grew angry, and said to the Witch,
“Give me back my shoe!”
s.note: תַּחְזִירִי is a future form used as a command, which is how most Israelis give orders and requests in speech; the formal imperative is הַחְזִירִי. הֶחְזִיר (hif'il) = to give back, the causative of חָזַר (to come back).

s.line: “I will not,” retorted the Witch,
s.note: הֵשִׁיב (hif'il) = to reply, a more formal word than עָנָה; it also means "to return, give back": הֵשִׁיב אֶת הַכֶּסֶף. Hebrew often answers a yes-no question by repeating the verb: לֹא אַחְזִיר = "I won't (give it back)".

s.line: “for it is now my shoe, and not yours.”
s.note: <t>נַעַל</t> is feminine, so "it is" is <t>זוֹ</t> (or <t>זֹאת</t>), not <t>זֶה</t>. In casual speech many people say <t>זֶה</t> for everything.

s.line: “You are a wicked creature!” cried Dorothy.
s.note: קָרָא = to cry out, call; the same verb means "to read" and "to name". Context decides: קָרְאָה סֵפֶר = she read a book, קָרְאוּ לוֹ דָּנִי = they called him Danny.

w: אֵין לָךְ|you have no|~lit. there is not to you
s.line: “You have no right to take my shoe from me.”
s.note: זְכוּת = a right: זְכוּיוֹת אָדָם (human rights), זְכוּת הַצְבָּעָה (the right to vote). It can also mean merit or credit: בִּזְכוּתְךָ = thanks to you.

s.line: “I shall keep it, just the same,” said the Witch, laughing at her,
s.note: צָחַק עַל = to laugh at, make fun of; צָחַק מִ־ = to laugh at a joke, and צָחַק עִם = to laugh with. בְּכָל זֹאת = nevertheless, even so. אֶצְלִי = with me, at my place: הַמַּפְתֵּחַ אֶצְלִי = I have the key.

s.line: “and someday I shall get the other one from you, too.”
This made Dorothy so very angry that she picked up the bucket of water that stood near and dashed it over the Witch,
s.note: הִכְעִיס (hif'il) = to make angry, the causative of כָּעַס (to be angry): זֶה מַכְעִיס אוֹתִי = it makes me angry.

w: מִכַּף רֶגֶל וְעַד רֹאשׁ|from head to foot|~idiom: from sole of foot to head
s.line: wetting her from head to foot.
s.note: מִכַּף רֶגֶל וְעַד רֹאשׁ = from head to toe; Hebrew goes the other way, from the sole of the foot to the head. נִרְטַב (nif'al) = to get wet: נִרְטַבְתִּי בַּגֶּשֶׁם = I got soaked in the rain.

s.line: Instantly the wicked woman gave a loud cry of fear,
and then, as Dorothy looked at her in wonder, the Witch began to shrink and fall away.
s.note: הִתְכַּוֵּץ = to shrink, contract; a cramp is הִתְכַּוְּצוּת, and clothes shrink in the wash: הַחֻלְצָה הִתְכַּוְּצָה. הִתְפּוֹרֵר = to crumble, fall apart, also of a political coalition. הִבִּיט בְּ־ = to look at, with בְּ־.

s.line: “See what you have done!” she screamed.

w: עוֹד רֶגַע|in a moment|~idiom: another moment
s.line: “In a minute I shall melt away.”
s.note: עוֹד רֶגַע = in a moment, any second now; רֶגַע! alone = wait a second! נָמֵס (nif'al) = to melt: הַגְּלִידָה נְמַסָּה = the ice cream is melting; its future is יִמַּס, אֶמַּס.

s.line: “I’m very sorry, indeed,” said Dorothy,
s.note: מִצְטַעֵר = sorry; in hitpa'el the ת swaps places with a first root letter צ and turns into ט, so it is not מִתְצַעֵר. Dorothy says the feminine מִצְטַעֶרֶת.

s.line: who was truly frightened to see the Witch actually melting away like brown sugar before her very eyes.
s.note: מַמָּשׁ = really, literally, actually; in speech it is a very common intensifier: מַמָּשׁ יָפֶה = really beautiful, מַמָּשׁ עַכְשָׁיו = right now.

s.line: “Didn’t you know water would be the end of me?” asked the Witch, in a wailing, despairing voice.
s.note: מַיִם (water) is plural in Hebrew: מַיִם יִהְיוּ, הַמַּיִם קָרִים. מְיֹאָשׁ = in despair, hopeless, a pu'al participle; יֵאוּשׁ = despair, and אַל תִּתְיָאֵשׁ! = don't give up!

s.line: “Of course not,” answered Dorothy.
“How should I?”
s.note: אָמוּר לְ־ + infinitive = supposed to; it is the pa'ul participle of אָמַר, so literally "said to": הָרַכֶּבֶת אֲמוּרָה לְהַגִּיעַ בְּשֵׁשׁ = the train is supposed to arrive at six. בָּרוּר שֶׁלֹּא = of course not, and בָּרוּר! = sure, obviously.

s.line: “Well, in a few minutes I shall be all melted, and you will have the castle to yourself.
s.note: בְּעוֹד + a time = "in, after": בְּעוֹד שָׁעָה = in an hour, בְּעוֹד שָׁבוּעַ = a week from now.

s.line: I have been wicked in my day,

w: וְלָשִׂים סוֹף|and put an end|~idiom: put an end
s.line: but I never thought a little girl like you would ever be able to melt me and end my wicked deeds.
s.note: הֵמֵס (hif'il) = to melt something, the causative of נָמֵס (to melt by itself). לָשִׂים סוֹף לְ־ = to put an end to: צָרִיךְ לָשִׂים לָזֶה סוֹף = this has to stop.

s.line: Look out—here I go!”
With these words the Witch fell down in a brown, melted, shapeless mass and began to spread over the clean boards of the kitchen floor.
s.note: קָרַס = to collapse, a news word for buildings, bridges and systems: הַבִּנְיָן קָרַס, הַבּוּרְסָה קָרְסָה. חֲסַר + noun = "-less": חֲסַר צוּרָה (shapeless), חֲסַר בַּיִת (homeless). הִתְפַּשֵּׁט = to spread, as a fire or an illness does; the same word also means to get undressed.

s.line: Seeing that she had really melted away to nothing,
Dorothy drew another bucket of water and threw it over the mess.
s.note: לִכְלוּךְ = dirt, mess; the verb is לִכְלֵךְ (to make dirty) and the adjective מְלֻכְלָךְ (dirty), a pu'al participle.

s.line: She then swept it all out the door.
After picking out the silver shoe, which was all that was left of the old woman,
she cleaned and dried it with a cloth, and put it on her foot again.
s.note: יִבֵּשׁ (pi'el) = to dry something, while הִתְיַבֵּשׁ (hitpa'el) = to dry up by itself, as the Witch's blood did. נָעֲלָה = put on (a shoe); Hebrew needs no "on her foot".

s.line: Then, being at last free to do as she chose,

w: שֶׁבָּא הַקֵּץ|that the end had come|~idiom: the end came
הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמַּעֲרָב|the Wicked Witch of the West
s.line: she ran out to the courtyard to tell the Lion that the Wicked Witch of the West had come to an end,
s.note: רָצָה here is "she ran" (from רָץ), stressed on the last syllable. Without vowels it looks exactly like רָצָה "he wanted" (stressed on the first syllable); "she wanted" is רָצְתָה. בָּא הַקֵּץ עַל = the end has come for, a literary phrase.

s.line: and that they were no longer prisoners in a strange land.
s.note: כְּבָר לֹא = no longer, not anymore: אֲנִי כְּבָר לֹא גָּר שָׁם = I don't live there anymore. זָר = foreign, strange; עוֹבְדִים זָרִים = foreign workers.
